one_paragraph_summary: Two threads in one column: Charter change and the ICC follow-up. On Cha-cha, CJ Panganiban brands the House's 301-6-1 con-con resolution a 'sneaky attempt to overhaul, not just amend or revise, the Constitution' -- turning on Rep. Rufus B. Rodriguez's TV-interview admission to Karen Davila that, once convened, a con-con cannot be limited to economic provisions and may install a federal-parliamentary system and 'infinite term extensions for lawmakers and other politicians.' If economic liberalization is the genuine goal, the proper route is a constituent assembly with the three-fourths vote 'voting separately' -- using Sen. Robinhood Padilla's 'laser surgery' metaphor -- and avoiding the multibillion-peso cost of con-con delegate elections, salaries, per diems, allowances, and transportation. If a con-con must be convened, transparency demands openly adopting CJ Reynato S. Puno's full Consultative Commission recommendations including federalism (even though CJ himself disagrees) rather than disguising the overhaul. The political-economy reality is that 'Cha-cha cannot succeed without the support of PBBM' and 'dancing is not one of his priorities,' compounded by SP Migz Zubiri's announcement that Cha-cha is not a Senate priority -- so 'the music and noise of Cha-cha, whether sneaky or open' should stop for now. On the ICC follow-up to A115, CJ reports support from 'a top judiciary incumbent, a brilliant Cabinet member, and several other readers' for the independent-panel proposal modeled on Ferdinand Marcos Sr.'s 1983 Agrava Board (with Narvasa and Tan Jr. as general-counsel templates), and answers the common objection -- 'are there enough independent and credible citizens?' -- with concrete name-lists: 13 retired jurists fit to head the panel (Abad, Azcuna, Bellosillo, Perlas-Bernabe, Callejo Sr., Carandang, Del Castillo, Gutierrez, Jardeleza, Mendoza, Reyes Jr., Minerva Reyes, Vitug), 31 nominees from business/professions/youth/NGOs, and 7 candidates for the two general-counsel slots (Bautista, Concepcion, Divina, Espinosa, Poblador, Prodigalidad, Villanueva). The column closes with CJ's ethical self-recusal: he declined a Supreme Court incumbent's nomination of him to head the panel because 'Ethically, I should not benefit from my own proposal.'
